author: Jakson Gudawela
headline: Carbon capture has a technical track now because the Gulf has projects to argue about
deck: CCUS appears at GOTECH as an engineering discipline rather than a policy discussion, which is what happens once contracts are awarded.
excerpt: Carbon capture, utilisation and storage forms a declared GOTECH track, reflecting Gulf projects that have moved from commitment into construction.
content:
Carbon capture, utilisation and storage is one of the declared technical tracks at GOTECH in Dubai at the end of September. Its presence on a peer-reviewed engineering programme rather than in a policy session marks a transition: the regional conversation has moved from whether to capture carbon to how to engineer the plant that does it.

The projects behind that shift are substantial. This publication has reported QatarEnergy awarding Samsung C&T a 4.1 million tonne carbon capture project at Ras Laffan, and ADNOC's programme alongside its wider award pipeline. Those are construction contracts, not commitments, and they create a body of engineers with the same problems to solve.

The Gulf's position in carbon capture is genuinely advantageous, for reasons that have little to do with climate ambition. Capture is cheapest where the carbon dioxide stream is concentrated and the source is a single large point — which describes gas processing, ammonia and hydrogen production far better than it describes power generation or cement. The region has a great deal of exactly that kind of plant. Storage requires deep formations with proven containment, and decades of oil and gas activity have characterised the subsurface more thoroughly than almost anywhere else on earth.

Utilisation is where the regional case diverges from the European one. Enhanced oil recovery — injecting carbon dioxide into a producing reservoir to mobilise additional oil — gives the captured stream a commercial value rather than a disposal cost. That transforms project economics and it complicates the accounting, because the process produces hydrocarbons whose eventual combustion has to be set against the carbon stored.

The engineering problems the track addresses are specific: capture solvent selection and degradation, compression and dehydration for pipeline transport, materials selection for streams that become highly corrosive in the presence of water, well integrity for injection over decades, and monitoring to demonstrate the carbon has stayed where it was put. That last item is where capture meets the asset integrity discipline covered at STATIC Arabia earlier this month, and it is a permanent obligation rather than a project one.

The presence of national oil company chief executives on the same programme's plenary — from ADNOC Onshore and Offshore, EGPC, Dragon Oil and Sharjah National Oil Corporation — puts the strategic and technical conversations in the same building, which is the argument for an operator-led technical conference.

Programme detail is taken from SPE's published technical programme. What the sessions may usefully settle is how much of the region's announced capture capacity has a confirmed storage destination behind it.
